Abstract—The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has 
exacerbated data privacy risks, necessitating rigorous compliance 
auditing of IoT companion application privacy policies. However, 
automated detection faces unique technical challenges, such as 
complex cross-paragraph dependencies and semantic conflicts 
between devices and applications. Traditional NLP methods lack deep 
reasoning capabilities, while single Large Language Models (LLMs) 
suffer from inherent reasoning biases and hallucination risks, failing 
to ensure strict legal traceability. To bridge this gap, we propose an 
evidence-traceable, multi-agent collaborative compliance detection 
framework driven by heterogeneous LLMs. First, we construct a fine-
grained evaluation paradigm based on the Personal Information 
Protection Law (PIPL) and employ an indicator-driven Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism to strictly anchor model 
reasoning to traceable policy fragments. Second, we design an 
evidence-quality-driven dynamic routing mechanism via a Task 
Complexity Assessment Model (TCAM), which adaptively dispatches 
multiple heterogeneous LLM agents based on quantitative difficulty 
and evidence scarcity, achieving an optimal balance between 
computational overhead and robustness. Furthermore, an Iterative 
Robust Aggregation (IRA) and consistency verification module is 
introduced to filter single-model biases and map identified risks to 
specific legal provisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the 
proposed framework achieves expert-level diagnostic precision with 
an average accuracy of 92.5%, a Macro-F1 of 93.3%, and a Cohen's

Abstract—The proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT) has 
exacerbated data privacy risks, necessitating rigorous compliance 
auditing of IoT companion application privacy policies. However, 
automated detection faces unique technical challenges, such as 
complex cross-paragraph dependencies and semantic conflicts 
between devices and applications. Traditional NLP methods lack deep 
reasoning capabilities, while single Large Language Models (LLMs) 
suffer from inherent reasoning biases and hallucination risks, failing 
to ensure strict legal traceability. To bridge this gap, we propose an 
evidence-traceable, multi-agent collaborative compliance detection 
framework driven by heterogeneous LLMs. First, we construct a fine-
grained evaluation paradigm based on the Personal Information 
Protection Law (PIPL) and employ an indicator-driven Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism to strictly anchor model 
reasoning to traceable policy fragments. Second, we design an 
evidence-quality-driven dynamic routing mechanism via a Task 
Complexity Assessment Model (TCAM), which adaptively dispatches 
multiple heterogeneous LLM agents based on quantitative difficulty 
and evidence scarcity, achieving an optimal balance between 
computational overhead and robustness. Furthermore, an Iterative 
Robust Aggregation (IRA) and consistency verification module is 
introduced to filter single-model biases and map identified risks to 
specific legal provisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the 
proposed framework achieves expert-level diagnostic precision with 
an average accuracy of 92.5%, a Macro-F1 of 93.3%, and a Cohen's 
Kappa of 0.85. Meanwhile, it accelerates the auditing efficiency by 
approximately 30 times compared to manual reviews, supporting high-
throughput processing at 168 documents per hour. This end-to-end 
auditable system provides a highly scalable and interpretable 
regulatory technology (RegTech) solution for privacy governance in 
massive IoT ecosystems. 
Index Terms— large language model, Internet of Things, 
privacy policy, compliance detection, multi-agent system, 
retrieval-augmented generation, Personal Information Protection 
Law.

B. Dataset and Evaluation Indicator System Construction
Dataset construction: We constructed a corpus of privacy
policies for IoT companion mobile applications in a specific 
domain. The corpus was manually collected to reflect real-
world deployments and compliance practices in heterogeneous 
IoT scenarios. The dataset consists of 100 privacy policies, 
classified into three representative categories: smart 
monitoring applications (27 policies), dashcam applications 
(37 policies), and smart home applications (36 policies). These 
categories were chosen because they typically involve 
continuous sensing, cross-device data flows, and frequent 
third-party SDK integrations, which increase the complexity 
of compliance and auditing.

the retrieved evidence set, that is, it fully follows the prompt 
word templates in Table I, and outputs a structured JSON object 
that contains the evidence audit results and the difficulty

The generation of this JSON object strictly follows the role 
and task specifications defined in Table III. First, for each 
secondary indicator, the router evaluates the evidence status as 
strong, medium, weak, or missing based solely on the retrieved 
evidence set, and simultaneously outputs a short quotation from 
the original policy text as a traceable citation anchor. These 
short quotations play a critical role in the framework: they not 
only expose missing elements, vague wording, and potential 
contradictions directly at the source level, but also preserve the 
minimal yet locatable textual basis required for downstream 
verification, cross-model comparison, and post-hoc auditing. In 
this way, uncertainty is not hidden behind an abstract label, but

is instead grounded in auditable fragments of the original 
document. Second, rather than assigning the overall difficulty 
level through qualitative prompt rules such as “most” or “many” 
secondary indicators being sufficiently supported, the router 
aggregates the secondary-indicator evidence signals under the 
proposed Task Complexity Assessment Model (TCAM) and 
computes the quantitative complexity score 𝜃௜ . The final 
difficulty level is then determined by thresholding 𝜃௜, yielding 
the corresponding routing state of easy, moderate, or difficult 
in a formally reproducible manner. This structured JSON 
output, rather than a direct compliance conclusion, is used as 
the downstream scheduling signal. Specifically, when the 
routing result is easy (𝜃௜ < 0.4), only one evaluation model is 
activated for lightweight assessment; when it is moderate 
( 0.4 ≤ 𝜃௜ < 0.7), three evaluation models are activated in 
parallel to balance robustness and computational overhead; and 
when it is difficult (𝜃௜ ≥ 0.7), five evaluation models are jointly 
scheduled to better handle sparse evidence, ambiguous wording, 
cross-paragraph dependencies, and potential clause conflicts. 
By tightly coupling prompt engineering with quantitative 
routing, the system transforms evidence auditing, citation 
grounding, and inference-budget allocation into a unified and 
auditable control process.
